summary: Specifies the semantics of a Middlebox Communication (MIDCOM) protocol, which lets agents talk to middleboxes like firewalls and NATs. It gives the meaning of the operations but not a concrete syntax or transport. It replaces RFC 3989. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Firewalls are gatekeepers. This describes what an outside helper can say to a gatekeeper, like open this door for this guest, without choosing the exact words.

subtitle: The abstract set of operations an agent can use to ask a firewall or NAT to open, reserve and close paths for traffic.

tldr.problem: Applications that need dynamic firewall or NAT configuration had no standard way to ask the middlebox for it, and the MIDCOM working group needed a shared definition of what such requests mean.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines transactions between an agent and a middlebox: session control, policy rules that either reserve or enable addresses and ports, and optional groups of rules, each with lifetimes and state machines.
tldr.outcome: It gives only semantics, with no concrete syntax or transport, so a real MIDCOM protocol must implement these semantics or a superset of them. It obsoletes RFC 3989.

today: RFC 5189 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2008. It obsoletes RFC 3989, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines semantics only, not a wire protocol.

sections.title: What MIDCOM Semantics Cover
sections.content:
The MIDCOM working group defined a framework and a list of requirements for talking to middleboxes. This RFC takes the next step: it specifies the semantics of a MIDCOM protocol, meaning what each operation means and how the middlebox state changes. It is aimed at packet filters and Network Address Translators (NATs) and supports applications that need them configured dynamically.

The semantics are defined as transactions. A request transaction is a request from the agent, processing at the middlebox, and a reply. It is either a configuration transaction (asks for a state change) or a monitoring transaction (asks for state information and changes nothing). An asynchronous transaction is not triggered by an agent; the middlebox sends notification messages to affected agents.

No concrete syntax or transport protocol is specified. A real protocol is expected to implement these semantics or, more likely, a superset, and may add transactions or parameters or split one transaction into several.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a list of the polite requests you can make to a gatekeeper, like open this door or tell me who is allowed in. It does not say what language to speak.

sections.title: General Protocol Design
sections.content:
Every request carries an agent-unique request identifier so the agent can match replies to requests. The protocol has three message kinds: request, reply and notification. Negative replies are the same for every transaction: the request identifier plus a failure reason. There are three notification types: the Session Termination Notification (STN), the Policy Rule Event Notification (REN) and the Group Event Notification (GEN).

All request transactions are atomic with respect to each other. Processing is never interrupted by another request, nothing starts until the whole request arrives, and no intermediate state is reported. Asynchronous transactions may interrupt or end processing at any time.

Access control is by ownership: the owner of a policy rule is the authenticated agent that established it, and all rules in one group must have the same owner. How the middlebox is configured to let other agents, for example an administrator, touch those rules is out of scope.

At session setup the middlebox reports its capabilities, such as firewall and NAT functions, wildcard support, supported IP versions, which optional transactions are offered, rule persistence, idle timeout, the maximum rule lifetime and the maximum number of simultaneous sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: Every request has a ticket number, so answers can be matched to questions. Each request is handled all at once, never half done, and only the person who made a rule can change it.

sections.title: Sessions
sections.content:
Before any rule can be created, the agent and middlebox need a MIDCOM session, an authenticated and authorized association. Agents start sessions; either side can end them. Three transactions handle this: Session Establishment (SE), Session Termination (ST) and Asynchronous Session Termination (AST).

For mutual authentication, two SE transactions are used. The first carries a middlebox challenge (mc); the reply carries the middlebox authentication (ma) and an agent challenge (ac). The second SE carries the agent authentication (aa). Authentication can instead be provided by other means, for example TLS or IPsec, in which case one SE transaction is enough. The successful reply includes the middlebox capabilities. Failure reasons include authentication failed, no authorization, protocol version mismatch and lack of resources.

When a session ends, by ST, by AST or by a broken connection, the middlebox keeps all established policy rules until their lifetime expires or an event ends them.

The session state machine starts in CLOSED. A successful SE with a challenge moves it to NOAUTH; a second successful SE moves it to OPEN. If authentication was already provided, one successful SE goes straight to OPEN.
sections.plainLanguage: First the helper and the gatekeeper check each other's ID cards. Only then can the helper ask for anything. If the helper leaves, the doors it opened stay open until their timers run out.

sections.title: Policy Rules and Groups
sections.content:
A policy rule binds one action to a condition describing a set of packets. In MIDCOM the action is always either reserve or enable. A Policy Reserve Rule (PRR) reserves an IP address, or an address plus a range of ports, on neither, one or both sides of the middlebox, and changes no packet handling. A Policy Enable Rule (PER) actually changes packet handling: on a NAT it creates bindings, on a firewall it opens pinholes, and on a combined device it does both. A PER can use an earlier PRR reservation or create a rule from scratch.

Each rule has a middlebox-unique identifier, an owner and a lifetime. The Policy Rule Lifetime Change (RLC) transaction can extend or shorten a lifetime, and a lifetime of zero deletes the rule. The granted lifetime is at most the smaller of the requested lifetime and the maximum the middlebox stated at session setup. The Policy Rule List (PRL) and Policy Rule Status (PRS) transactions are monitoring transactions that list rules and report their properties.

Each rule belongs to exactly one policy rule group. If the agent names no group, the middlebox creates one. A group exists only while it has members. Group Lifetime Change (GLC) acts like an RLC on every member, and Group List (GL) and Group Status (GS) let an agent explore groups, which helps when a replacement agent takes over after a failure.

When a rule changes state or lifetime, the requesting agent gets the reply and every other agent who can access the rule and has an open session gets a REN message.
sections.plainLanguage: A reserve rule is like putting a Reserved sign on a table. An enable rule is actually letting your guests in. Each rule has a timer, and you can bundle rules into a group to change all their timers at once.

sections.title: Address Tuples
sections.content:
Rules describe addresses using address tuples: IP version, IP address, prefix length, transport protocol, port number, port parity and port range. Four tuples describe a connection through the middlebox:

  • A0: the internal endpoint.
  • A1: the middlebox inside address.
  • A2: the middlebox outside address.
  • A3: the external endpoint.

For a firewall, A2 equals A0 and A1 equals A3. For a traditional NAT, A2 differs from A0 and A1 equals A3. For a twice-NAT, both A1 and A2 are assigned by the NAT.

The semantics cover IPv4 and IPv6, and TCP and UDP; other transports such as SCTP are left to concrete protocols. The IP address can be wildcarded using the prefix length, depending on local middlebox policy. The transport protocol can be TCP, UDP or ANY. A port number of zero means wildcard, and the port range gives a number of consecutive ports (1 means a single port). Port parity can be odd, even or any in a PRR, and same or any in a PER. A direction of flow of inbound, outbound or bidirectional says where traffic may start.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a mail room. There are the real sender and receiver, plus two desk labels the mail room uses on each side. A rule says which labels go with which person.

sections.title: The Policy Rule State Machine
sections.content:
Each policy rule identifier (PRID) has its own state machine. Everything starts in PRID UNUSED, meaning the rule does not exist or is not active. A successful PRR moves it to RESERVED. A successful PER moves it to ENABLED, either from RESERVED or directly from PRID UNUSED with no reservation.

Successful RLC transactions with a lifetime above zero keep a rule in RESERVED or ENABLED. An asynchronous rule event (ARE), or a successful RLC with lifetime zero, returns it to PRID UNUSED, after which the middlebox may reuse the identifier. A failed request changes no state. GLC transactions can cause the same transitions as RLC.
sections.plainLanguage: A rule is like a seat at a restaurant: free, then reserved, then used by guests, then free again when the timer runs out or someone cancels.

sections.title: Conformance
sections.content:
A protocol definition complies if it includes all the specified transactions with their mandatory parameters. Session control, PRR, PER, RLC, PRL, PRS and the asynchronous transactions are mandatory. The group transactions GLC, GL and GS are optional. A compliant implementation MUST support all mandatory transactions, MAY support none, one or more of GLC, GL and GS, and MAY add transactions or parameters, or replace one transaction with several finer-grained ones, provided the set stays equivalent to the single transaction and keeps its atomicity.

Interface-specific policy rules are optional; if supported, either both or neither of the inside and outside interface parameters MUST be included. A middlebox must tell the agent which transactions it supports during SE, and an agent must not use an optional transaction the middlebox does not support.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a must-do list and a nice-to-have list. Everyone must do the first list, and you only ask for the nice-to-haves if the gatekeeper says it offers them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Letting an outside entity configure a middlebox seems to contradict what a middlebox is for, so the RFC requires mutual authentication, authorization, message integrity and message confidentiality. The semantics define mutual authentication in SE and rely on underlying protocols such as TLS or IPsec for integrity and confidentiality.

Wildcards are the main risk. A rule with the IP address set to any address would make the middlebox useless for security, and local policy should reject such a request. A reasonable default is that only one port number may be wildcarded and no IP address may be. The RFC notes that some SIP applications using early media need the other party's address wildcarded before it is known, so the operator must decide how to balance function against security.

Section 7 also addresses the IAB's UNSAF concerns. It argues that MIDCOM is a long-term solution rather than a workaround, because endpoints are not involved in allocating or deleting addresses and ports; the MIDCOM server has full control.
sections.plainLanguage: Letting a helper reopen your front door is risky, so the gatekeeper checks who is asking and refuses a request like let everybody in.

items.label: Session Termination
items.desc: Configuration; mandatory. Agent closes the session.

items.label: Asynchronous Session Termination
items.desc: Asynchronous; mandatory. Middlebox ends the session.

items.label: Policy Reserve Rule
items.desc: Configuration; mandatory. Reserves addresses and ports.

items.label: Policy Enable Rule
items.desc: Configuration; mandatory. Creates NAT bindings or pinholes.

items.label: Policy Rule Lifetime Change
items.desc: Configuration; mandatory. Extends, shortens or deletes a rule.

items.label: Policy Rule Status
items.desc: Monitoring; mandatory. Reports one rule's properties.

items.label: Asynchronous Policy Rule Event
items.desc: Asynchronous; mandatory. Notifies agents of rule changes.

items.label: Group Lifetime Change
items.desc: Configuration; optional. Changes lifetimes of a whole group.

items.label: Group List
items.desc: Monitoring; optional. Lists groups the agent can access.

items.label: Group Status
items.desc: Monitoring; optional. Lists a group's member rules.
